questions.stem: In the AWS shared responsibility model, what does "security of the cloud" refer to?

options.text: Protecting the data that a customer stores in Amazon S3
options.rationale: Customer data is part of security in the cloud, which the customer manages.

options.text: Protecting the infrastructure that runs AWS services
options.rationale: AWS is responsible for the hardware, software, networking and facilities that run AWS Cloud services.

options.text: Configuring permissions for IAM users and roles
options.rationale: Access permissions are set by the customer, so they are security in the cloud.

options.text: Choosing the encryption keys for objects in a bucket
options.rationale: Amazon S3 encrypts new objects by default, and the customer chooses the encryption type and keys, such as SSE-KMS, so this is security in the cloud.

questions.explanation: AWS owns security of the cloud (the infrastructure); the customer owns security in the cloud (what they build and store on it).

questions.stem: A company launches Amazon EC2 instances for a web application. Which task is the company's responsibility?

options.text: Controlling physical access to the data center
options.rationale: AWS secures the facilities where the service operates.

options.text: Maintaining the hypervisor on the host servers
options.rationale: AWS operates the virtualization layer and the host operating system.

options.text: Configuring security group rules for the instances
options.rationale: The customer configures the AWS-provided firewall, called a security group, for each instance.

options.text: Replacing failed hardware in the physical host servers
options.rationale: AWS maintains the hardware that runs EC2.

questions.explanation: EC2 is infrastructure as a service, so the customer configures what runs on and around each instance: its security groups, guest operating system and software. The facilities, hypervisor and hardware belong to AWS.

questions.stem: Which task is the responsibility of AWS under the shared responsibility model?

options.text: Securing the facilities where AWS services run
options.rationale: Physical security of AWS data centers is part of security of the cloud.

options.text: Applying updates to a customer's guest operating system
options.rationale: Guest operating system patching is the customer's job on EC2.

options.text: Deciding which users can read an S3 bucket's objects
options.rationale: Access permissions are applied by the customer with IAM.

options.text: Choosing which key encrypts a DynamoDB table
options.rationale: DynamoDB encrypts all data at rest, and the customer chooses which AWS KMS key type protects each table.

questions.explanation: AWS operates and controls everything from the host operating system and virtualization layer down to the physical security of the facilities.

questions.stem: Besides the AWS service a company uses, which factors help determine the company's security responsibilities?

options.text: The instance sizes and the number of Availability Zones used
options.rationale: Capacity and placement choices affect cost and availability, not who is responsible for security.

options.text: The AWS Support plan and the billing account structure
options.rationale: Support and billing arrangements do not change the responsibility split.

options.text: The network bandwidth and latency to the chosen Region
options.rationale: Performance characteristics do not decide security responsibilities.

options.text: Data sensitivity, company requirements and applicable laws
options.rationale: AWS documentation lists these as factors that, together with the service used, shape the customer's responsibilities.

questions.explanation: Responsibility depends on the service chosen and on the customer's own data, requirements and legal obligations.

questions.stem: Some controls in the shared responsibility model are shared: AWS applies them to its infrastructure, and the customer applies them to its own resources. Which is an example of a shared control?

options.text: Physical and environmental protection
options.rationale: AWS alone protects its data centers, so the customer fully inherits this control.

options.text: Patch management
options.rationale: AWS patches its infrastructure, and the customer patches its own guest operating systems and applications.

options.text: Classifying the customer's data
options.rationale: Classifying data is the customer's responsibility, whichever service is used.

options.text: Maintaining the hypervisor
options.rationale: The virtualization layer is run by AWS alone.

questions.explanation: The clue is that both parties do the same kind of work, each on its own layer: AWS patches the infrastructure and the customer patches its guest operating systems and applications. Physical protection is different because AWS does all of it and the customer simply inherits it.

questions.stem: Which type of control does a customer fully inherit from AWS?

options.text: Awareness and training for the customer's staff
options.rationale: AWS trains AWS employees, so the customer must train their own.

options.text: Patch management of the guest operating system
options.rationale: Patching is a shared control, and the guest operating system layer is the customer's.

options.text: Configuration management of customer databases
options.rationale: The customer configures their own databases and applications.

options.text: Physical and environmental controls
options.rationale: AWS manages the facilities, so the customer inherits these controls.

questions.explanation: Inherited controls are those a customer takes entirely from AWS, with physical and environmental controls as the standard example.

questions.stem: A company moves a self-managed database from Amazon EC2 to Amazon RDS. Which task does AWS take over?

options.text: Applying software patches to the database engine
options.rationale: Amazon RDS is a managed service that handles backups, software patching, failure detection and recovery.

options.text: Defining which IAM users can reach the database
options.rationale: The RDS documentation notes that customers control access with IAM users and permissions, so this stays with the customer.

options.text: Classifying the data stored in the database
options.rationale: Knowing and classifying their data is always the customer's job.

options.text: Writing the application code that queries the data
options.rationale: Application code is the customer's responsibility.

questions.explanation: Managed services move more of the stack to AWS. The customer still controls access, data and application code.

questions.stem: Why does a company have fewer security tasks when it stores data in Amazon S3 than when it runs servers on Amazon EC2?

options.text: S3 data is kept in a different Region from EC2 instances
options.rationale: Region choice does not change who is responsible for what.

options.text: Amazon S3 is outside the shared responsibility model
options.rationale: The model applies to every AWS service.

options.text: AWS runs the operating system and platform for S3
options.rationale: For abstracted services such as S3, AWS operates the infrastructure, operating system and platforms; on EC2 the customer manages the guest operating system.

options.text: Paying for S3 storage moves the security duties to AWS
options.rationale: Payment does not transfer responsibility; customers still manage their data and permissions.

questions.explanation: The clue is the type of service: EC2 is infrastructure as a service, so the customer manages the guest operating system and everything above it, while S3 is an abstracted service where AWS runs those layers. In both, the customer still manages its data and permissions.

questions.stem: Which TWO tasks are the customer's responsibility when a company stores data in Amazon S3? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Managing the stored data, including encryption options
options.rationale: Customers manage their data and choose how it is encrypted.

options.text: Operating the storage infrastructure behind the service
options.rationale: AWS operates the infrastructure layer for S3.

options.text: Using IAM tools to apply appropriate permissions
options.rationale: Access to buckets and objects is controlled by permissions the customer sets.

options.text: Maintaining the operating system the service runs on
options.rationale: For abstracted services AWS operates the operating system and platforms.

options.text: Providing physical security for the data centers
options.rationale: Facility security is part of security of the cloud.

questions.explanation: For abstracted services such as S3, customers are responsible for their data, classifying their assets, and using IAM to apply permissions.

questions.stem: For an abstracted service such as Amazon DynamoDB, which layers does AWS operate?

options.text: The infrastructure, operating system and platforms
options.rationale: For abstracted services, AWS runs the infrastructure, operating system and platforms; customers only use the service endpoints to store and retrieve data.

options.text: The facilities, but not the operating system
options.rationale: AWS also operates the operating system and platforms for abstracted services.

options.text: The application code that reads and writes the tables
options.rationale: Application code is written and secured by the customer.

options.text: The IAM policies attached to the tables
options.rationale: Permissions on the customer's resources are applied by the customer.

questions.explanation: Abstracted services shift the lower layers to AWS, leaving the customer with their data, its classification and access permissions.

questions.stem: A company runs code on AWS Lambda. Which is the company's responsibility?

options.text: Patching the operating system that runs the functions
options.rationale: AWS manages the operating system for Lambda.

options.text: The function code and the permissions it is granted
options.rationale: Customers secure their code, its dependencies and its IAM execution role.

options.text: Managing the servers in the Lambda fleet
options.rationale: AWS manages the underlying servers.

options.text: Scaling the infrastructure that runs functions
options.rationale: Lambda scales automatically.

questions.explanation: With Lambda, AWS manages the infrastructure and runtime environment; the customer manages code, data and access.

questions.stem: For Amazon RDS, which task is AWS responsible for?

options.text: Creating database users and granting their permissions
options.rationale: Database users and permissions are configured by the customer.

options.text: Writing the security group rules that allow access
options.rationale: Network access rules are the customer's to configure.

options.text: Managing the underlying host operating system
options.rationale: AWS manages the underlying infrastructure and host operating system for RDS.

options.text: Deciding whether to enable encryption for the database
options.rationale: Encryption choices are made by the customer.

questions.explanation: On RDS the customer still manages database access, network rules and encryption settings.

questions.stem: A company runs applications on Amazon EC2. Who installs security patches on the guest operating system?

options.text: AWS, as part of running the EC2 service
options.rationale: AWS patches the host operating system and virtualization layer under the instance, not the guest operating system inside it.

options.text: AWS Support, after the company opens a case
options.rationale: AWS Support gives guidance; it does not sign in to or patch customer instances.

options.text: The company running the instances
options.rationale: On EC2 the customer controls the guest operating system, so installing its updates and security patches is the customer's job.

options.text: AWS and the company together
options.rationale: Patch management is shared, but it is split by layer: the guest operating system layer belongs to the company alone.

questions.explanation: The clue is "guest operating system": that is the OS inside the instance, which the customer chooses and controls, so the customer patches it. AWS patches the host operating system and virtualization layer underneath, and it patches the OS for you on managed services such as Amazon RDS.

questions.stem: Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for classifying data and deciding who can access it?

options.text: The customer, for any AWS service
options.rationale: Customers own their data, its classification and its access control on every service.

options.text: AWS, when a managed service is used
options.rationale: Managed services move infrastructure duties to AWS, not data decisions.

options.text: AWS, for data stored in Amazon S3
options.rationale: S3 data and its access are still the customer's responsibility.

options.text: AWS and the customer share it equally
options.rationale: Data classification and access are the customer's alone.

questions.explanation: Responsibility for infrastructure shifts by service, but data and access always stay with the customer.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for securely destroying storage devices when they reach the end of their life in AWS data centers?

options.text: The customer whose data was on the device
options.rationale: Customers have no access to physical devices in AWS data centers.

options.text: AWS
options.rationale: Decommissioning and destroying media in AWS facilities is part of security of the cloud.

options.text: An external auditor chosen by the customer
options.rationale: Auditors review controls; they do not destroy media.

options.text: The customer, for Amazon EBS volumes
options.rationale: Customers delete volumes; AWS handles the physical media.

questions.explanation: Physical and environmental controls, including media handling, are inherited from AWS.

questions.stem: Which task is the customer's responsibility under the shared responsibility model?

options.text: Securing the hypervisor on the host servers
options.rationale: The virtualization layer belongs to AWS.

options.text: Controlling who can enter AWS data center buildings
options.rationale: Facility access belongs to AWS.

options.text: Encrypting data on the client side before upload
options.rationale: Encryption choices for the customer's data are customer responsibilities, and client-side encryption runs on the customer's own systems.

options.text: Maintaining the AWS global network backbone
options.rationale: The global network belongs to AWS.

questions.explanation: The clue is "client side": that encryption happens on the customer's own systems before the data reaches AWS, so it is security in the cloud. The other three options are parts of the infrastructure that AWS runs.

questions.stem: Which is part of security of the cloud, which AWS is responsible for?

options.text: Passwords for the company's IAM users
options.rationale: IAM credentials are managed by the customer.

options.text: Bucket policies on the company's Amazon S3 buckets
options.rationale: Bucket policies are set by the customer.

options.text: The company's own application code
options.rationale: Application code is the customer's responsibility.

options.text: The data centers in each Availability Zone
options.rationale: The global infrastructure, including the data centers that make up each Availability Zone, is part of what AWS protects.

questions.explanation: AWS protects the infrastructure: hardware, software, networking and the facilities of its global infrastructure.

questions.stem: As a company moves from self-managed software on Amazon EC2 to services such as Amazon DynamoDB, how does its share of security responsibility change?

options.text: It decreases, because AWS runs more of the stack
options.rationale: Abstracted services leave the customer with fewer layers to manage.

options.text: It increases, because managed services need more setup
options.rationale: Managed services reduce, not increase, the customer's layers.

options.text: It stays exactly the same for every service
options.rationale: Responsibility varies by service.

options.text: All of it moves to AWS
options.rationale: Customers keep responsibility for their data and access on every service.

questions.explanation: The customer still manages data, classification and IAM permissions on abstracted services.

questions.stem: A company configures network traffic protection, such as firewall rules and how traffic is routed in its VPC. Under the shared responsibility model, whose responsibility is this?

options.text: AWS's, because the VPC runs on AWS hardware
options.rationale: AWS runs the infrastructure; you configure your network on it.

options.text: The customer's
options.rationale: Network and firewall configuration is listed as a customer responsibility.

options.text: The internet service provider's
options.rationale: ISPs do not configure customer VPCs.

options.text: Shared equally, rule by rule
options.rationale: Customers write and maintain their own rules.

questions.explanation: Security groups, network ACLs and route tables are configured by the customer.

questions.stem: Which TWO are AWS responsibilities under the shared responsibility model? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Choosing encryption settings for data in Amazon S3
options.rationale: Encryption choices are the customer's.

options.text: Maintaining the virtualization layer
options.rationale: AWS operates the host operating system and virtualization layer.

options.text: Patching the guest operating system on Amazon EC2
options.rationale: The guest OS is the customer's responsibility.

options.text: Physical security of data centers
options.rationale: Facility security is part of security of the cloud.

options.text: Writing IAM policies for the company's users
options.rationale: IAM policies are customer-managed.

questions.explanation: AWS: security of the cloud. Customer: security in the cloud.
